claims.text: Atomic-size mismatch produces severe lattice distortion in HfNbTaTiZr.
Lattice distortion stabilizes a single-phase BCC structure in HfNbTaTiZr.
Lattice distortion creates high intrinsic stress fields in HfNbTaTiZr.
Deformation of HfNbTaTiZr is dominated by screw-dislocation glide at lower temperatures.
Increasing temperature causes HfNbTaTiZr to cross over from screw-dominated to edge-dislocation-mediated plasticity.
High lattice friction supports screw-dislocation glide at lower temperatures, with that glide becoming progressively thermally activated.
Edge-dislocation glide at elevated temperature is less temperature-sensitive and more strongly influenced by severe lattice distortion than screw glide.
The screw-to-edge transition limits further reductions in the yield strength of HfNbTaTiZr at elevated temperature.
HfNbTaTiZr should exhibit a yield-strength plateau or reduced rate of yield-strength change at elevated temperature.
The screw-to-edge transition produces a plateau or reduced rate of change in the elastic modulus of HfNbTaTiZr.
The dislocation-mode transition reduces lattice anharmonicity.
Reduced lattice anharmonicity caused by the dislocation transition produces a lower-than-expected thermal-expansion coefficient.
The edge-dislocation density relative to the screw-dislocation density should increase as temperature rises.
The relevant elevated-temperature response is expected to occur within approximately 800°C to 1600°C.
The initial as-cast HfNbTaTiZr material is homogeneous, single-phase BCC, and minimally segregated.
The proposed mechanism applies only while HfNbTaTiZr remains homogeneous and single-phase BCC without significant segregation or precipitation.
Processing-induced microstructural heterogeneity or grain-boundary precipitation can alter the mechanical response of alloys in the HfNbTaTiZr system.
Conventional BCC refractory alloys show monotonically decreasing strength and elastic modulus with temperature because screw dislocations remain controlling.
